title: Scalable financing mechanisms for pure public goods

concept.text: Conceptual synthesis: The proposed innovation is a practical way to mobilize and allocate substantial financing for pure public goods: goods whose benefits are non-rival, so one person’s use does not diminish another’s, and non-excludable, so withholding benefits from nonpayers is infeasible. The mechanism would turn dispersed willingness to support a shared benefit into durable funding, while eliciting useful information about which projects participants value. It remains a proposed capability rather than a demonstrated financing system.

Conceptual synthesis: Free riding and private information create distinct problems. People may receive benefits without contributing, and organizers generally cannot directly observe how much each person values provision. Whether participants gain by misstating their valuations depends on the mechanism; misreporting is not an unavoidable feature of every design. A credible proposal must specify who contributes, who decides what gets funded, how payments depend on participants’ reports or actions, and which incentive, participation and budget assumptions it accepts.

significance.text: Conditional significance: A mechanism that generated substantial, durable additional resources and allocated them usefully could expand the public goods that decentralized financial arrangements can support. The revolutionary advance would require a demonstrated improvement in the scale and effectiveness of financing, beyond the existence of a formally interesting payment rule or a successful small deployment. Additionality matters: redirecting existing donations or relying on an uncounted subsidy would not by itself demonstrate an expansion of available resources.

Conditional applications and limits: Basic research and pandemic preparedness are plausible beneficiaries, particularly where their benefits extend well beyond the organizations or people paying for them. These activities can also include private, excludable or locally concentrated benefits, so an application must identify the public-good component it actually finances. Better funding could enable more research or preparedness, but scientific progress, effective execution and political coordination would still require separate successes. Mobilizing contributions also does not automatically establish fair representation or socially desirable allocation.

missing_breakthrough.text: Synthesis of the research and review: The missing capability is an operational financing mechanism that sustains useful provision at consequential scale despite free riding, private information and strategic behavior. The design must make explicit its treatment of truthful reporting, efficient provision, voluntary participation, budget balance and collusion. These objectives should not be presented as simultaneously guaranteed across arbitrary settings. Their compatibility depends on the information structure, preferences, participation rules and other assumptions; the supplied evidence does not establish a particular impossibility theorem or a general solution.

Proposed engineering agenda: A workable system would need to translate its formal assumptions into enforceable participation and payment rules, identify the source of any subsidy, and account for administration and verification costs. It would also need to withstand coordinated manipulation and assess whether reported willingness to pay gives disproportionate influence to participants with greater resources. A rule that performs well with a small, selected group may behave differently with heterogeneous participants, repeated funding rounds and beneficiaries who never participate. Establishing those practical boundaries is part of the breakthrough.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a historical theoretical precursor: Jerry Green, Elon Kohlberg and Jean-Jacques Laffont’s “Partial Equilibrium Approach to the Free-Rider Problem,” dated November 1976 in the supplied metadata, with DOI 10.1016/0047-2727(76)90049-9. The research attributes to pages 375–376 an analysis of truthful mechanisms, a rebate approach, and relationships between incentive properties and budget balance under specified assumptions. However, the source index records the PDF as not captured and contains no retained text or artifacts. The supplied review therefore could not verify those page-level attributions, the document’s content-based identity or its completeness. They remain reported historical contributions rather than independently checked findings in this record.

Evidence scope: Even if the historical attribution is confirmed, a theoretical mechanism under specified assumptions would not establish a globally scalable voluntary financing system. The supplied materials contain no verified field deployments, quantitative funding gains, operating costs, durability measurements or comparative allocation results. They also contain no freshness search record supporting an assessment of developments through the review’s stated cutoff of November 1, 2026. The record consequently cannot establish the latest frontier or confirm that the practical capability remains open at that date. These limitations do not show that the historical result is false or that the proposed innovation is incoherent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Publish a sufficiently precise mechanism specification to permit independent implementation and assessment. It should define eligible goods, participants and beneficiaries; the information collected; contribution and allocation rules; participation rights; and the source and treatment of external funding. Formal claims should identify their assumptions and distinguish individual truthfulness from resistance to coordinated manipulation. Budget accounting should include subsidies, rebates, administrative expenses and any obligations carried into later funding rounds.
completion_criteria.label: Independently implementable mechanism specification with full budget accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed field evaluation: Conduct independently evaluated deployments involving consequential public goods and diverse participants, using credible alternatives as comparators. Measure net additional funding, persistence across repeated funding cycles, useful allocation and delivery of the financed goods. Account for displacement of existing contributions, subsidies, manipulation, unequal representation and administrative costs. Funding totals alone would be insufficient if resources were allocated poorly or the apparent gains disappeared after full costs were included.
completion_criteria.label: Independent deployments demonstrate durable net funding with effective allocation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: Define scale, duration and success thresholds before evaluation, with thresholds appropriate to the intended application. Independent teams should be able to reproduce the central results and test sensitivity to participant composition, funding conditions and strategic behavior. To substantiate revolutionary significance, the evidence would need to show a material magnitude and breadth of improvement, not merely feasibility. These are proposed criteria rather than established standards; finite deployments could establish demonstrated breadth and operating limits, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce material, broad improvements against predefined thresholds

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: FIN-09, “Causal measurement of investment’s financial and real-world impact,” overlaps through evaluation: FIN-10 needs evidence that its mechanism causes additional financing and useful outcomes. FIN-09 concerns causal measurement, while FIN-10 concerns the rules that mobilize and allocate resources. FIN-05, “Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories,” also addresses underfunding, but its stated focus is creditworthiness and missing conventional records; FIN-10 addresses shared benefits that can accrue to nonpayers.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-03, “Run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment,” could matter when financed public goods require long commitments, but funding stability and free riding are distinct problems. FIN-04, “Low-cost, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods,” concerns risk protection; public-good financing could complement prevention efforts without replacing insurance. FIN-06, “Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer,” and FIN-07, “Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money,” could provide useful payment infrastructure, but convenient or private transfers alone do not establish incentives to finance shared benefits.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-01, “A general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior,” and FIN-11, “Operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage,” share concerns about information and behavior, while addressing different financial questions from public-good provision. FIN-02, “Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades,” and FIN-08, “A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes,” concern financial instability. Some prevention efforts might themselves generate widely shared benefits, creating a possible application for FIN-10; financing them would still leave their causal and predictive challenges unresolved. These relationships are inferred from the supplied roster titles, not from separate assessments of those concepts.

unresolved_issues: The attributed analysis on pages 375–376 of the 1976 paper remains unverified because no retained source text or artifacts were supplied.
The materials do not establish the current practical frontier or whether the proposed capability remains unsolved through November 1, 2026.
No particular mechanism is specified, leaving its information requirements, incentive guarantees, participation rules, budget treatment and collusion assumptions unresolved.
Scale, duration, comparator selection and success thresholds for a convincing deployment remain to be defined.
The record supplies no verified quantitative evidence of additional funding, allocation quality, durability, costs or representation effects.
The intended applications still require a precise account of which benefits qualify as pure public goods and which are private, excludable or locally concentrated.

brief.title: Lasting funding for benefits everyone can share
possible: People could sustain projects whose benefits everyone can enjoy without reducing anyone else’s share, including people who never pay. Contributions would help reveal which projects people value and turn scattered support into substantial, lasting funding.
why: Basic research and pandemic preparedness could gain resources for benefits that extend far beyond those paying. More funding could support more research and preparedness.
Communities could support a wider range of shared projects through decentralized funding. Success would mean expanding the resources available and directing them toward useful work.

sources.who: Jerry Green, Elon Kohlberg and Jean-Jacques Laffont
sources.showed: This is a theoretical study of truthful reporting, rebates and balancing payments against spending in funding shared benefits.
sources.cited_for: It provides a theoretical precursor addressing incentives and funding budgets.
sources.not_established: A theoretical payment rule does not establish a practical system that sustains substantial funding.

sources.who: Vitalik Buterin, Zoë Hitzig and E. Glen Weyl
sources.showed: Their quadratic funding rule uses sponsor money to amplify contributions, rewarding broad support. They prove that it produces optimal funding under their model’s assumptions.

sources.not_established: The model does not establish lasting additional resources or effective allocation under real budgets and coordinated manipulation.

sources.cited_for: It identifies budget constraints and strategic behavior that practical funding rules must handle.
sources.not_established: Reciprocal contributions alone do not prove manipulation, and these rounds do not establish performance across diverse settings.

sources.not_established: Deployment and simulations do not establish durable net additional funding or independently reproduced benefits across communities.

sources.quote: we find revenue gains are available on both margins.

sources.not_established: A raffle experiment does not establish lasting funding or useful allocation for widely shared benefits.

shown: Gitcoin has put sponsor-backed funding rules into operation for shared projects. Miller, Weyl and Kanich combined deployment with interviews and simulations to assess a revised rule. Pasquini’s analysis of earlier rounds found practical limits from scarce sponsor funds and reciprocal giving.
missing: A fully specified system still needs to connect its assumptions to enforceable payment and participation rules, with every cost accounted for.
Independent deployments still need to demonstrate lasting additional funding after displaced donations, subsidies and operating costs are counted.
Evaluations still need to establish useful project selection and delivery while accounting for manipulation and unequal influence.
Independent teams still need to reproduce substantial improvements across different participants and funding conditions.

milestones.label: An independently implementable design with complete budget accounting
milestones.explanation: A specification would have to define participants, beneficiaries, information, payments, allocation, assumptions and all budget obligations. This would let independent teams implement and assess the system.

milestones.label: Independent deployments sustain additional funding and useful allocation
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluations would have to show lasting net funding gains and useful delivery against credible alternatives, accounting for costs and distortions. This would establish practical value at consequential scale.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce broad gains against predefined thresholds
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce substantial improvements across varied conditions against thresholds set in advance. This would establish the breadth of the gains and the system’s operating limits.

uncertain: Which combinations of honest reporting, voluntary participation, effective provision and balanced budgets can a practical design sustain?
How much influence would wealthier contributors gain, and how would people who benefit without participating be represented?
What scale, duration and size of improvement would establish success for each application?

page.title: Decentralized financing of pure public goods
page.definition: A financing mechanism mobilizes voluntary contributions and explicitly funded subsidies for pure public goods: benefits whose use by one person does not reduce another’s and from which nonpayers cannot be excluded. It increases net funding and provision across repeated funding rounds as participation grows.

goal.need: In 2023, the United Nations General Assembly cited health-emergency preparedness needs of approximately US$30 billion per year, including US$10 billion in new external financing annually. These are health-system totals, not a measured funding gap for pure public goods. OECD distinguishes financing health research from ensuring that its knowledge and products have non-rival, non-excludable benefits. The financing problem concerns the public-good components of these activities.

figures.caption: Annual health-emergency preparedness financing cited by the United Nations General Assembly in 2023
figures.note: The external financing gap is part of the total requirement. Neither figure isolates pure public goods.

statements.quote: mobilize additional timely, reliable, flexible, equitable, predictable and sustainable funding for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
statements.context: Paragraph 76 of resolution A/RES/78/3 calls for mobilization through existing financing tools, including multilateral development banks.

statements.quote: Long-term, we have a goal of $1 Billion in funds distributed through Allo protocol (IN PROGRESS)
statements.context: The strategy published on 5 February 2024 covers public goods and Ethereum ecosystem growth. Its distribution target does not specify net additional financing for pure public goods.

completion.title: Independent field studies reproduce net funding and provision gains as participation increases.
completion.criterion: A financing mechanism produces a positive causal increase, against existing fundraising, in both net resources devoted to identified pure public goods and delivered public-good benefits. The increase persists across repeated funding rounds and is reproduced independently with more participants. Accounting includes sponsor funds, displaced contributions, prizes, administration and verification; reallocating a fixed subsidy alone does not pass. Achievement is limited to the goods, participant numbers and duration tested.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external completion test for this combined capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches of UN/OECD reports, standards, prizes, AEA experiment registrations and developer programmes located no common scale, duration and net-additionality pass test for pure-public-good financing. Gitcoin’s US$1 billion target includes ecosystem grants. This fallback tests gains that persist and replicate as participation grows, without asserting universal scalability.

milestones.title: A funding rule increases laboratory public-good provision after incentive costs against voluntary giving.
milestones.criterion: Public-good provision exceeds a voluntary-contribution benchmark after accounting for incentive costs and equalizing the fundraiser’s external financial commitment. Corazzini, Faravelli and Stanca tested lotteries and all-pay auctions with 144 participants, 48 per treatment, in groups of four over 20 rounds. Across all rounds, provision was about 20% higher for lotteries and 3.5% higher for auctions than the benchmark.
milestones.set_by: Experimental public-goods research; Corazzini, Faravelli and Stanca (2010), Hypothesis 1 and Table 5. This is a published experimental benchmark, not a field-wide certification.
milestones.threshold_quote: Both LOT and APA outperform VCM, not only in terms of gross contributions, but also after taking into account the cost of the prize.

milestones.title: A live funding round distributes contributions and sponsor funds to public-good projects.
milestones.criterion: An operating funding round collects voluntary contributions and transfers sponsor matching funds to projects under its published allocation rule. Gitcoin’s February 2019 deployment dedicated US$25,000 to open-source projects. The study submitted on 22 September 2025 reports that 32 of 38 Gitcoin rounds used connection-oriented quadratic funding or hybrids, distributing about US$4 million. Its welfare comparison used simulations with 25 agents. These results establish funding operations, without verifying pure-public-good provision by every recipient.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; Gitcoin publishes its funding-round procedure, but no general pure-public-good deployment pass test was located.

milestones.title: A field deployment increases net funding and public-good provision across repeated funding rounds.
milestones.criterion: Against existing fundraising, a mechanism increases net resources reaching an identified pure public good and its delivered benefits across repeated rounds, accounting for sponsor finance, displaced giving and operating costs. No cited study establishes this combined result. A 2015 working paper, not peer reviewed, reports 849 household decisions in April 2014 and US$6.23 per solicitation for a convex raffle; its poverty-relief beneficiary was not verified as a pure public good. Pasquini identifies constrained matching funds and reciprocal backing in Gitcoin data.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches located comparative fundraising endpoints and repeated deployments, but no published pass threshold combining pure-public-good provision, net additional financing and persistence.

not_found: No external completion threshold was located that combines scale, duration, net additional financing and delivered pure-public-good benefits.
No independent field replication was located that establishes the combined completion criterion as participation increases.
The supplied Toulouse repository PDF for Green, Kohlberg and Laffont returned HTTP 404, preventing verification of its page-level claims.
